title: The hoopoe's news
hookLine: a small bird brings Sulayman news of a queen who worships the sun (27:20–26)

lines: A ROLL CALL OF THE BIRDS.
cards: Sulayman is inspecting the birds, one by one, like a commander walking a line of troops. And there's a gap. Why don't I see the hoopoe, he asks.
Is it absent? The hoopoe is a striking little bird, cinnamon-colored, with a crest that fans open like a crown and wings barred black and white. Sulayman isn't pleased.
He'll punish it severely, he says, unless it brings a clear excuse. Not long after, the hoopoe lands.

teach.b: Its first words are astonishing, given who it's talking to. In the Arabic: I have encompassed what you have not encompassed.
Pickthall renders the next words: "I come unto thee from Sheba with sure tidings." A bird the size of your hand tells the man who speaks to birds and commands jinn that it knows something he doesn't.
Then it reports carefully, like a good scout. A woman rules the people of Saba', Sheba.

teach.h: A QUEEN, A THRONE, THE SUN.
teach.b: She's been given something of everything, and she has a great throne. The hoopoe saw her and her people bowing to the sun instead of God, because Shaytan had made their deeds look fair to them.

It even adds a short reflection of its own, about God who brings out what is hidden in the heavens and the earth. Now look at Sulayman. He doesn't wave the bird away because it's small, or punish it for speaking boldly.

teach.h: WE SHALL SEE IF YOU SPEAK TRUTH.
teach.b: He doesn't simply believe it either: we shall see whether you have told the truth or are one of the liars. And he sends the hoopoe back with a letter.
That's the shape of the scene: listen to the small voice, then check it. Some commentators tell a story that the hoopoe could sense water underground, and that the army relied on it.
That's from later commentary, not the verse. The verse gives enough: a king who noticed one bird missing, and a bird who came back knowing something he didn't.

how: Muslims read the hoopoe's story in Surah An-Naml as a lesson in listening carefully and verifying news, and the hoopoe is among the creatures a hadith says not to kill.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose voice usually gets passed over: a child at the table, the newest person at work, the quiet one in the group chat, the person who cleans the building.
Ask yourself what they might know that you don't, and hold that question kindly for a minute. If you pray, you can ask for the humility to be told something new.
